blocks.content: A laptop with a browser, a music player, and a code editor open at once feels like it is doing everything simultaneously, but a single processor core is only ever executing one instruction stream at a time. The illusion of multitasking is created, moment by moment, by the operating system pausing whatever process is currently running and handing the processor to another one so cleanly that neither process ever notices the gap. That precise act of pausing one and resuming another is called a context switch.

This chapter explains exactly what a context switch is, the exact sequence of steps the operating system performs to carry one out, why it costs real time and is never free, how switching between two processes differs from switching between two threads of the same process, and why an operating system works to avoid triggering more of them than it has to.
1. The Illusion of Multitasking

Even a machine with several processor cores usually has far more runnable processes than it has cores to run them on. To create the appearance that everything is progressing at once, each core is rapidly handed from one process to the next, giving each one a short turn before moving on. A context switch is the mechanism behind every single one of those handoffs.

blocks.title: Why the gaps are invisible to you
blocks.content: A modern processor can perform a context switch in a matter of microseconds, and a timer interrupt can trigger dozens or hundreds of switches every second. Human perception cannot register a gap that short, so a machine juggling many processes still feels perfectly smooth to the person using it, even though only one instruction stream is actually executing on a given core at any instant.
2. What a Context Switch Actually Is
blocks.text: 2. What a Context Switch Actually Is

blocks.content: A context switch is the act of saving the complete execution state of the process or thread currently occupying the CPU, then loading the previously saved execution state of a different process or thread, so that the second one can resume running from the exact instruction where it was last paused, as though no interruption had ever happened.

A context switch is saving exactly where you were so the CPU can be handed to someone else, and later loading exactly where that someone else was, so both can eventually resume as if nothing had interrupted them at all.

The word context here refers to the minimum information needed to resume a process correctly: its program counter, marking the next instruction to execute, and the full set of CPU register values it was using. As the process control block chapter already covered, this saved information is written into and later read back out of the PCB assigned to each process. A context switch does not move any of a process instructions or data in memory, only this small snapshot of register and program counter values travels between the hardware and the PCB.
3. The Step by Step Sequence of a Context Switch
blocks.text: 3. The Step by Step Sequence of a Context Switch

blocks.content: Every context switch follows the same basic sequence, whether it is triggered by a timer, an I/O request, or a scheduling decision.

["Something signals that a switch is needed: a timer interrupt marking the end of the current time slice, the running process making a blocking I/O request, or a higher priority process suddenly becoming ready to run.","The processor traps into the kernel, handing control over to the operating system rather than continuing to execute the interrupted process.","The scheduler determines that the process currently occupying the CPU, process A, must give it up.","The operating system copies the current CPU register values and program counter out of the hardware and saves them into the PCB of process A, then updates the state field of A, typically from running to ready or waiting.","The scheduler runs its selection logic over the ready queue and picks the next process to run, process B, then locates the PCB of process B.","The operating system loads the saved register values and program counter out of the PCB of process B back into the actual CPU registers.","The state of process B is updated to running, and the processor resumes execution at exactly the instruction its program counter points to, exactly where B had previously been paused."]
items: Something signals that a switch is needed: a timer interrupt marking the end of the current time slice, the running process making a blocking I/O request, or a higher priority process suddenly becoming ready to run.
The processor traps into the kernel, handing control over to the operating system rather than continuing to execute the interrupted process.
The scheduler determines that the process currently occupying the CPU, process A, must give it up.

The operating system copies the current CPU register values and program counter out of the hardware and saves them into the PCB of process A, then updates the state field of A, typically from running to ready or waiting.
The scheduler runs its selection logic over the ready queue and picks the next process to run, process B, then locates the PCB of process B.
The operating system loads the saved register values and program counter out of the PCB of process B back into the actual CPU registers.
The state of process B is updated to running, and the processor resumes execution at exactly the instruction its program counter points to, exactly where B had previously been paused.

blocks.content: Notice the symmetry in this sequence. Everything that leaves the CPU is written into a PCB, and everything that enters the CPU is read back out of a PCB. This is exactly why a process can be interrupted in the middle of an instruction sequence and, potentially much later, continue as though no time had passed for it at all.
4. Why a Context Switch Is Not Free
blocks.text: 4. Why a Context Switch Is Not Free

blocks.content: From the point of view of the process being switched in or out, a context switch feels instantaneous. From the point of view of the machine as a whole, it costs real, measurable time, and that cost comes from two different places.
The direct time cost

Trapping into kernel mode, saving register values, updating scheduler data structures, and restoring register values all consume actual processor cycles, typically somewhere in the range of low single digit microseconds on modern hardware. During that entire window, neither the outgoing process nor the incoming process is making any forward progress on its own work. That time is pure overhead, spent entirely on the mechanics of switching rather than on anything either process actually asked the computer to do.
Cache pollution

The bigger cost is often indirect. While process A was running, the processor cache filled up with data and instructions that A was actively using, making the cache warm for A. The instant process B resumes, that cache is still full of data belonging to A, not B, so the cache is cold for B. Many of the memory accesses B makes right after resuming will miss the cache and fall through to much slower main memory, until B own working set gradually pushes A data out and the cache warms up again for B. This effect is called cache pollution, and it can quietly cost far more total time than the direct save and restore step.

blocks.title: Why switching too often hurts throughput
blocks.content: If context switches happen so frequently that no process ever runs long enough to build a warm cache before being switched out again, the processor spends most of its time paying the direct switching cost and suffering repeated cache misses, rather than doing useful work for anyone. This condition is sometimes described as thrashing on the scheduler, and it is a real risk if time slices are set too short.
5. Process Switch Versus Thread Switch

Not every context switch costs the same amount. Switching the CPU between two entirely separate processes is more expensive than switching it between two threads that belong to the same process, and the reason comes down to memory.

{"headers":["Aspect","Switch Between Two Processes","Switch Between Two Threads of the Same Process"],"rows":[["CPU registers and program counter","Saved and restored","Saved and restored"],["Memory address space mapping","Must be switched to the new process own page table","Shared already, this step can be skipped entirely"],["Relative cost","More expensive","Cheaper, often called a lightweight context switch"],["Cache and translation state","Address translation caches are typically flushed or invalidated","Address translation caches often remain valid across the switch"]]}

Threads that belong to the same process share the exact same virtual address space, meaning the same page table and the same memory mappings. Because of that, the expensive step of reloading the memory mapping hardware, and the associated cost of invalidating cached address translations, can simply be skipped during a thread switch. Registers and the program counter still have to be saved and restored for each thread individually, but the memory management overhead that makes a full process switch relatively costly is largely avoided.
6. Why the Operating System Tries to Minimize Unnecessary Context Switches
blocks.text: 6. Why the Operating System Tries to Minimize Unnecessary Context Switches

blocks.content: Since every context switch carries a direct time cost plus the indirect cost of cache pollution, cutting down on switches that do not need to happen directly increases how much real work the machine gets done in a given amount of time.

["Schedulers choose a time slice length carefully: long enough that a process gets meaningful work done and its cache stays warm, but short enough that the whole system still feels responsive to every other waiting process.","A compute heavy process that is clearly making steady progress is often allowed to keep running rather than being switched out prematurely, since interrupting it early would throw away a cache that has just become warm.","A very large number of short lived processes, or interrupts arriving in rapid succession, can indirectly force far more switching than a workload with fewer, longer running processes.","A voluntary context switch, where a process gives up the CPU willingly because it is blocked on I/O, is comparatively cheap to plan for, since the scheduler already knows that process has nothing useful to do until its I/O completes anyway."]
items: Schedulers choose a time slice length carefully: long enough that a process gets meaningful work done and its cache stays warm, but short enough that the whole system still feels responsive to every other waiting process.

A compute heavy process that is clearly making steady progress is often allowed to keep running rather than being switched out prematurely, since interrupting it early would throw away a cache that has just become warm.
A very large number of short lived processes, or interrupts arriving in rapid succession, can indirectly force far more switching than a workload with fewer, longer running processes.

A voluntary context switch, where a process gives up the CPU willingly because it is blocked on I/O, is comparatively cheap to plan for, since the scheduler already knows that process has nothing useful to do until its I/O completes anyway.

blocks.content: 7. A Worked Example
It helps to trace one concrete context switch from beginning to end to make the abstract sequence feel tangible.

["Process A is running, midway through a loop, with its working values sitting in the actual CPU registers.","The hardware timer fires an interrupt, marking the end of the time slice that had been given to A.","The processor traps into kernel mode and jumps to the operating system interrupt handler responsible for scheduling.","The operating system copies the exact register contents and current program counter of A into the PCB of process A, updates the state of A from running to ready, and places its PCB back onto the ready queue.","The scheduler examines the ready queue, applies whatever selection policy it uses, and selects process B, which had been waiting.","The operating system locates the PCB of process B and loads the register values and program counter that were saved there back into the actual CPU registers.","The state of process B is updated to running, and the CPU resumes execution at exactly the instruction B program counter pointed to, exactly where B had previously stopped."]
items: Process A is running, midway through a loop, with its working values sitting in the actual CPU registers.
The hardware timer fires an interrupt, marking the end of the time slice that had been given to A.
The processor traps into kernel mode and jumps to the operating system interrupt handler responsible for scheduling.

The operating system copies the exact register contents and current program counter of A into the PCB of process A, updates the state of A from running to ready, and places its PCB back onto the ready queue.
The scheduler examines the ready queue, applies whatever selection policy it uses, and selects process B, which had been waiting.
The operating system locates the PCB of process B and loads the register values and program counter that were saved there back into the actual CPU registers.
The state of process B is updated to running, and the CPU resumes execution at exactly the instruction B program counter pointed to, exactly where B had previously stopped.

blocks.content: From the perspective of process A, time simply skipped forward. It has no memory of anything happening while it was sitting on the ready queue. From the perspective of process B, the same thing happens in reverse: it resumes as though it had been paused only an instant ago, unaware that any time passed at all, because every register value it depends on was restored to precisely what it expects.
8. Common Misconceptions
A few misunderstandings about context switching come up often enough to call out directly.

["Assuming a context switch is instantaneous or free. It costs real, measurable processor time to save and restore state, and it very often costs additional time afterward due to cache pollution.","Assuming only the operating system pays the cost. Both the outgoing and the incoming process lose usable CPU time, since every cycle spent on the mechanics of switching is a cycle not spent on either process own instructions.","Assuming every context switch costs the same amount. Switching between two threads of the same process is cheaper than switching between two separate processes, because shared memory mappings mean the expensive address space reload can be skipped.","Assuming more context switching always means more effective multitasking. Excessive, unnecessary switching lowers total throughput, since overhead and repeated cold cache misses eat into the CPU time that could otherwise go toward real work."]
items: Assuming a context switch is instantaneous or free. It costs real, measurable processor time to save and restore state, and it very often costs additional time afterward due to cache pollution.

Assuming only the operating system pays the cost. Both the outgoing and the incoming process lose usable CPU time, since every cycle spent on the mechanics of switching is a cycle not spent on either process own instructions.

Assuming every context switch costs the same amount. Switching between two threads of the same process is cheaper than switching between two separate processes, because shared memory mappings mean the expensive address space reload can be skipped.

Assuming more context switching always means more effective multitasking. Excessive, unnecessary switching lowers total throughput, since overhead and repeated cold cache misses eat into the CPU time that could otherwise go toward real work.

blocks.content: 9. The Interview Angle

A context switch question in an interview almost always chains directly off the process control block. The strong answer names precisely what gets saved, the program counter and the full set of CPU register values, and precisely where it gets saved, into the PCB belonging to the outgoing process, then loaded back out of the PCB belonging to the incoming process. From there, the answer should go further than the save and restore mechanics alone: mention that a context switch is never free, citing both the direct cost of performing the save and restore and the indirect, often larger cost of cache pollution once the incoming process resumes with a cold cache. Mentioning that a switch between two threads of the same process is cheaper than a switch between two separate processes, because the address space mapping does not need to change, is a strong signal of real depth rather than a memorized definition.

If you can explain a context switch as a symmetric save into one PCB and restore from another, and can also name the real costs it carries beyond that save and restore, you are demonstrating the same depth of understanding that the process control block chapter builds toward.
